The title and authors Tuval Raz, Roni Reiter-Palmon, and Yoed N. Kenett match the document (rendered p. 1). The preprint, rather than the unread journal version of record, supports the screening results.

No randomized people study of generative-AI assistance is present. Studies 1 and 2 are human correlational task studies (design_class = other); Study 3 compares GPT-4 output with those human samples (design_class and context_class = ai_vs_human). The use of an LLM to score human responses is not AI assistance to participants (pp. 13-18, 25-27, 32-34).

Study 1 recruited 100 people, excluded 11 who supplied no AQT or AUT answers, and explicitly analyzed 89. Its reported demographics are 49.4% male and mean age 28.33; payment was 5 pounds. The 100 is not a randomized count (p. 13, Participants).

Study 2 reports 100 Prolific participants, 51% male, mean age 41.72, paid 5 pounds; the abstract also says N = 100. The exclusion rule has no numerical exclusion count, and the fluency comparison prints t(99). Keeping 100 as the reported human sample with the stated caveat is supported (pp. 2, 25-27). Both human samples exceed 50 people.

Study 3 reports 100 GPT-4 instances and no new human sample, using separate instances per task and the human samples from Studies 1 and 2 as comparators. The form correctly keeps its people n_randomized and n_analyzed null; AI sessions must not count toward a human sample threshold (pp. 32-34, Study 3).

The human tasks use AQT objects pencil, pillow, sock; AUT objects knife, purse, clock; 15 stumpers; and five CPS dilemmas. AQT and AUT allow two minutes per object. GPT-4 was prompted for 5-7 AQT/AUT responses without time limits; Appendix C contains the AQT prompt screenshot (pp. 13-18, 25-26, 33-34, 65-72).

Scoring matches the form: MAD semantic distance for AQT originality, OCSAI originality scoring for AUT, a fine-tuned GPT-2 model for CPS originality and quality, and first-author answer-key scoring for stumpers. The scored originality measures are not diversity across people (pp. 15-18, 26, 33-34).

S3-O1 reported statistics match the prose: GPT-4 CPS originality M = 2.28, SD = 0.32 versus human M = 2.2, SD = 0.37; t(100) = 0.75, p = .46, d = 0.151. This is no statistically significant difference, not evidence of equivalence (p. 37, AI vs. Humans).
S3-O2 reported statistics match the prose: GPT-4 CPS quality M = 3.6, SD = .18 versus human M = 2.82, SD = .22; t(100) = 11.8, p < .001, d = 2.36 (p. 37, AI vs. Humans).

S3-O3 reported statistics match the prose: GPT-4 AUT originality M = 3.28, SD = 0.25 versus Study 1 human M = 2.22, SD = 0.37; t(100) = 20.9, p < .001, d = 3.25. The additional Study 2 comparison also matches: human M = 2.32, SD = 0.55; t(100) = 15.5, p < .001, d = 2.19 (p. 36, AI vs. Humans).

S3-O4 reported statistics match the prose: GPT-4 AQT originality M = 0.94, SD = .006 versus Study 1 human M = 0.9, SD = .018; t(100) = 19.28, p < .001, d = 3. The additional Study 2 comparison also matches: human M = 0.89, SD = .021; t(100) = 19.54, p < .001, d = 2.76 (p. 36, AI vs. Humans).

S3-O5 reported statistics match the prose: GPT-4 stumper accuracy M = 9.1, SD = .68 versus human M = 3.9, SD = 2.66; t(100) = 16.62, p < .001, d = 2.58. The measure is the number of correct answers out of 15 (pp. 17-18 and 36, AI vs. Humans).

The one-line finding reproduces the prose values for AUT originality, CPS quality, and the nonsignificant CPS originality comparison. The source itself prints t(100) in every AI-human comparison; those labels are correctly preserved without recalculation (pp. 36-37, AI vs. Humans). Figure-label disagreements require the separate correction above.

This is a three-study empirical paper, not a synthesis; there are no pooled estimates or synthesis standardizers to extract, so synthesis defaults are appropriate. The authors declare no conflict of interest, and the document identifies no company participation (pp. 11-12, study overview; p. 50, Conflict of interest and Author contribution).
summary: No randomized human AI-assistance study is present; AI-versus-human context classification is correct. The reported statistics match the preprint prose, but the form needs corrections to randomization wording, unfinished fields, combined counts, outcome coverage, metadata, and unflagged figure discrepancies.
